A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HumanoidGen and HGen-Bench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures, tables, prompts and code examples, are readable and matchable despite reorganization and added experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation results for demonstration generation, MCTS reasoning, diffusion-policy learning and comparisons across LLM planners in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds physical-robot experiments, annotation-transfer measurements, challenging-task evaluations and resource measurements in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds a real-world adaptation: FoundationPose estimates object poses to initialize simulation, and generated trajectories are executed on the physical robot. The central atomic-operation, relational-constraint, collision-management and STCR/MCTS procedures remain unchanged. Automatic annotation migration was already described in v1.

E1.justification: V2 adds physical-robot evaluation of two retained tasks and five additional simulation scenarios: knob rotation, toaster pressing, safe-door opening, coordinated pot lifting and block stacking with barriers. Appendix C.2 also introduces quantitative annotation-transfer evaluation across sampled assets. These substantially broaden the evaluated environments and task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 6 introduces manual annotation as a timed comparator to automatic annotation migration, absent from v1's evaluation. The RoboTwin comparison, MCTS/non-MCTS comparison and four LLM-planner configurations are retained. The added discussion of augmentation frameworks does not provide new measured baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include real-world training with 5 or 25 real trajectories versus 100 simulated plus 5 real trajectories, evaluation over 20 trials, and physical-object pose randomization. Annotation evaluation samples 20 assets per category, while the five additional tasks have specified randomization ranges. The original benchmark training and MCTS settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds annotation-transfer accuracy and timing analysis with discussion of geometric failure cases, stage-by-stage resource analysis, and an obstacle-heavy stacking robustness test. The real-world study also tests the contribution of simulation data under limited real demonstrations. Existing MCTS-budget, plan-diversity and LLM-planner analyses remain.

E5.justification: The retained policy evaluations still report means and standard deviations using seeds 0, 1 and 2, and existing uncertainty displays are unchanged. New tables provide success counts or point estimates without introducing repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals or significance tests; their evaluation sample sizes are protocol additions.

E6.justification: The original numerical results in Tables 1–3 and the retained comparison plots are unchanged. V2 adds real-world collection success of 85% and 90%, and DP success of 65% and 70% with 100 simulated plus 5 real trajectories (Table 5). Tables 6–8 add annotation success of 90–100%, five-task success of 73–95.24%, and time/token measurements. These are newly reported results under additional conditions.

T1.justification: Scene-scaling Equation (4) changes from O alpha = O' alpha' for quantities expressed in the respective local frames to alpha' = T_{O→O'} alpha, with quantities now defined in the original and scaled scenes' world coordinates. This revises the formal coordinate specification. The constraint-solver and MCTS equations otherwise remain unchanged, with no new proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about automated bimanual demonstration generation, relational constraints, MCTS-enhanced reasoning, HGen-Bench and diffusion-policy data scaling. The introduction's central contributions also remain stable; the new appendix evidence supports rather than redefines them.

C2.justification: V1's limitations emphasize predefined primitives, long-horizon efficiency and the visual simulation-to-reality gap. V2 replaces this discussion with detailed manual-annotation requirements, stated restrictions on deformable/fluid simulation and dynamic-goal manipulation, and proposed extensions; the explicit visual-domain-gap caution is removed. It also adds interpretations of annotation failures, simulation pretraining and pipeline-stage reuse.

D1.justification: V2 adds deployment details including the head-mounted D435i camera at 640×480 resolution, FoundationPose initialization, annotation-evaluation asset sources and rendering software, and pipeline timing/token information. The original solver libraries, policy hyperparameters, prompt templates, substantive example code and project-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted positioning against augmentation methods, including DemoGen alongside DexMimicGen, and discusses learned annotation alternatives such as RoboBrain, CAP-Net and Dex1B. It also adds supporting technical references. The existing framework comparison and central novelty positioning remain; the dataset/benchmark survey is largely moved from the appendix into Section 4.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the appendices: MCTS joins the implementation section, experiments are regrouped and reordered into C.1–C.8, and a contents guide is added. The dataset/benchmark survey moves into the main related-work section. Relational-constraint exposition and limitations are rewritten, alongside smaller terminology, task-label and front-matter edits.

P2.justification: V2 adds real/sim scene panels, an annotation-migration grid and a challenging-task montage (Figures 9–11), plus four empirical/resource tables (Tables 5–8). Figure 3 gains explanatory action labels, and Figure 8's transformation arrows are revised. Existing displays are relocated, including the unchanged LLM comparison from Figure 9 to Figure 12.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked physical validation and quantitative tests of annotation efficiency. V2 addresses these gaps with real-robot transfer experiments, annotation accuracy/cost measurements, harder manipulation scenarios and resource accounting, while clarifying important applicability limits. These substantially strengthen practical validation. The physical study remains limited to two tasks, and C.3 claims baseline superiority without reporting comparator scores, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the evidence gains.
